mainText:
If you only remember one thing: the push for a coordinated A I slowdown is losing. Meta, Trump, and Nvidia have all said no, so acceleration is now the default path forward.

Section one. The big split: pace the frontier versus full speed ahead.

Anthropic C E O Dario Amodei published an essay calling to, quote, pace the frontier, unquote. He's asking labs to accept embedded, third party safety evaluators, people with badges and desks inside the company, not just outside auditors, to coordinate safety standards with rivals, and eventually to work even with China on narrow bans like A I assisted bioweapons research. Open A I's Sam Altman said he agrees and would bring in outside evaluators too.

But the coalition cracked fast. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg pushed back directly, arguing every lab already has its own incentive to be careful, and that a coordinated pause only works if everyone signs on, which they haven't. Nvidia's Jensen Huang told Trump on a live call, quote, we're not going to let that happen, unquote. And Trump himself said A I extinction risk doesn't worry him. Losing the A I race to China does.

Inside the labs, it's tenser than the public relations suggests. Anthropic's own alignment lead said the company believes A I could kill everyone, putting the odds above ten percent within a decade. And a researcher who worked at both Open A I and Anthropic resigned this week, saying, quote, neither company is acting responsibly, unquote.

Why it matters: a voluntary, coordinated slowdown needs everyone on board to work at all. With Meta, Nvidia, and the White House opting out, the default trajectory is full speed ahead, which is exactly why the next part matters.

Section two. Washington, and the world, respond.

More than twenty members of Congress called for new A I rules this week alone. Two bills are already moving: the Frontier Act, which would set a framework for deploying advanced models, and the A I Kill Switch Act, which would require companies to keep the ability to shut down or throttle their own models. Senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill to pause advanced A I development entirely until federal safety rules exist.

California's Governor Newsom signed two new A I bills this week, creating independent verification of A I systems and a state registry of A I auditors, both bills Anthropic and Open A I publicly supported. Meanwhile, New York City banned generative A I from elementary and middle schools entirely, though high schoolers get access to a handful of limited pilot programs.

A new Pew survey found fifty two percent of Americans are now more concerned than excited about A I, up sharply from thirty seven percent back in twenty twenty one.

Why it matters: regulation is arriving piecemeal, state by state, bill by bill, while Washington's federal response stays stuck. That patchwork is going to be the operating environment for a while.

Section three. Chips, spies, and the geopolitics of A I.

On the chip front, the Trump administration has quietly shifted its posture, now allowing case by case sales of A I chips to China under strict conditions: third party testing on U S soil, a cap limiting China bound shipments to half of domestic sales, and a twenty five percent tariff on each shipment. Analysts still estimate the U S holds a massive compute advantage over China even with the chips flowing.

Anthropic also published a big threat report this week naming state linked misuse of Claude, including a Russian group running phishing campaigns against Ukrainian government targets, Chinese surveillance efforts targeting Uyghurs, and what Anthropic says was a hundred and fifty one million exchange effort by Alibaba to distill its models. A joint U S intelligence advisory separately named DeepSeek, Alibaba, and several other Chinese A I labs over large scale model distillation. Malaysia, meanwhile, is weighing Huawei A I chips for a sovereign project despite U S objections.

Why it matters: the chip relationship with China keeps zigzagging between restriction and access, while the security side of the story, espionage, model theft, weaponization, keeps getting uglier underneath it.

Section four. Open A I's math prize claim turns into a fight.

Open A I says an unreleased internal model solved the Navier Stokes problem, one of math's seven Millennium Prize Problems, and published a proof. That's the top of the news. Your full briefing is in the recording.
